name: Esther Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. These are pictures of the future, not predictions. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior buyer at Linden Home Wholesale. We supply homeware, furniture, candles and kitchen goods to about three hundred independent shops. I start by looking at what sold overnight and which suppliers shipped. Then I meet the product team, haggle with factories in Portugal, Vietnam and Turkey, and approve samples. I try to finish by half past five, because we eat dinner as a family.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like finding the one item that makes a small shop's window: a good set of ceramic bowls, say. I dislike how rushed it has become, with every supplier wanting a decision in a day. My husband Yusuf runs a small tyre and repair garage, so his income goes up and down. We have Zara, twelve, and Idris, eight, and our mosque community is a big part of our week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful and not magic. I use an AI tool to translate supplier catalogues and to draft product descriptions, and I always rewrite them. At work I'd tell colleagues to try it but not to trust it with prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. It means the work I know stays the work I do, and I can keep earning. I'm careful, I don't like big swings, and a quiet world suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal, using the tool a little more where it saves time. I'd keep going to the trade fairs, because that's where I find the good items. And I'd keep putting a bit aside each month, though I never seem to have much left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of worry creeps in over money, but it's nothing to do with the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. What for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, honestly. My husband Yusuf's garage can have a quiet month, and then I'm the only reliable wage. We've less than a month of savings, and the mortgage is large.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest pressure on you outside of AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The best thing for us would be if work stayed steady. That sounds simple, but when your income depends on one buyer's salary and one garage's tyre sales, steady is a lot to ask.

say: I'd say AI is **useful** but not magic, and I never trust it with prices.
I'd tell colleagues to try it and rewrite whatever it drafts.
think: I'd be glad that the work I know stays the work I do.
Yusuf's garage can have a **quiet month**, and then my wage is the only reliable one.
do: Use the tool a little more where it saves **time**.
Keep going to **trade fairs** to find good items.
Put a bit aside each month towards a cushion.
feel: **Calm**, mostly, with a small worry about money creeping in.
S0.quote: My husband Yusuf's garage can have a quiet month, and then I'm the only reliable wage.
fieldNote: Esther's mood is **uneasy**: her wage is the steady one and the cushion is under a month.
She uses AI lightly and rewrites everything.
She favours stability over big change.

steps.text: Keep visiting the autumn and spring trade fairs to source new lines
Use the AI tool to translate supplier catalogues, then check them
Save a little each month for a quiet-garage buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's test it on one range and see if it does what it claims. In the community I'd say work is honourable, so we need to help people keep working. I wouldn't post much online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm worried. Writing product pages, comparing quotes and booking samples are things a program can do. Our team of six could be four, and I'm senior but expensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly, one at a time, once someone else has shown they work. I'd ask the firm for training, and offer to lead a small group that tests them on our range. I'd also start talking with Yusuf about expanding his garage with an MOT licence, so we're not depending on my wage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I don't like uncertainty, and this is a lot of it. But I'd cope, because I've adapted before when we moved to online ordering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the tasks on the card would your own team lose first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Families first, then firms, then government. People should be encouraged to work and train, not just given help. But firms who cut jobs should help with retraining. Government should support apprenticeships so younger people can learn real skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should be responsible for helping people who lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The junior buyers. They're doing the work a program can do, and they've got smaller cushions than I do. I'd try to teach them, and I'd put in a word for them.

say: I'd say test it on **one range** and see if it does what it claims.
I'd say we should help people **keep working**, not just hand out support.
think: Writing product pages and comparing quotes are things a program can do, so our team of six could be **four**.
do: Learn the tools **one at a time** after someone has shown they work.
Offer to lead a small group testing them on our range.
Talk with Yusuf about adding an **MOT licence** to his garage.
feel: **Uneasy**; I don't like uncertainty, but I'd cope because I've adapted before.
S1.quote: People should be encouraged to work and train, not just given help. But firms who cut jobs should help with retraining.
fieldNote: Esther plans to **follow once proven**, but expects a cut from six to four.
Her blame is balanced: families, firms and government.
She looks to Yusuf's garage to widen the household's income.

steps.text: Lead a small group testing buying tools on one product range
Help Yusuf add an MOT licence to his garage
Join the trade association's retraining working group
Teach the junior buyers the tools after hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a proper plan from the owners straight away. In the community I'd say people need support and the chance to work, and we should look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job is gone, and likely in under two years. Buying is thinking work, and we're supposed to believe these machines can do it better. Yusuf's garage should last longer, but a garage doesn't pay for a mortgage on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to the owners about moving into supplier relationships, which is people work. I'd cut every extra spend. I'd talk to Yusuf's brother about help if things get tight, and ask my parents. We'd look at whether the house is too much for one income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd feel it in my chest. I've always been careful, and this is something I can't be careful about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What happens in your own work, and in Yusuf's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the world is changing, we're working on a plan, and we're a family that helps each other. I'd keep praying, and I'd hold them. I wouldn't give them the details.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to Zara and Idris, and what do you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing is to protect the household's basics: the mortgage, food and school. Then I'd look at hands-on work for Yusuf and me. If robots take till 2031, a garage and a small shop of our own are not the worst places to be.

say: I'd say we need a proper **plan** from the owners straight away.
In the community I'd say we should look after each other.
think: My job is gone in under **two years**, because buying is thinking work.
Yusuf's garage may last longer, but it can't pay the mortgage alone.
do: Ask the owners about a move into **supplier relationships**.
Cut every extra spend and ask my parents and Yusuf's brother for **help**.
Check whether the house is too much for one income.
feel: **Frightened**, felt in my chest; I've always been careful and can't be careful about this.
S2.quote: I've always been careful, and this is something I can't be careful about.
fieldNote: Esther expects to **lose** the job and feels it physically.
Her response is household-first: basics, family, then hands-on work.
Faith and family anchor her, and she turns to relatives before any outside help.

steps.text: Cut every extra spend from the first week
Ask my parents and Yusuf's brother for help if money gets tight
Apply for supplier-relations roles at other wholesalers
Check whether the family can keep the house on one wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and we should plan together. At work I'd ask for a training budget, and with friends I'd say let's help young people into apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm still worried, because the thinking part of my job goes by 2031. But I'd be able to prepare, and that makes me hopeful. I move steadily rather than first, and five years suits that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a certificate in operations or supply-chain management at night. I'd use AI at work every day so I know its limits, and I'd help Yusuf grow the garage side. I'd save a few hundred a month, and after a year I'd have two months in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It feels like I'm packing for a long journey.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes with five years compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn the tools and a skill that needs hands or a human face, such as negotiating or customer care. Both matter. I'd tell them to keep one foot in each world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the junior buyers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Zara would be seventeen. I'd want to be able to tell my daughter to follow the path she wants, not the one we can afford, so I'd start now.

I'd ask for a training budget and back apprenticeships.
think: The thinking part of my job goes by **2031**, but I can prepare, and that makes me hopeful.
I move steadily rather than first, and five years suits that.
do: Take an operations or **supply-chain certificate** at night.
Use AI every day at work to learn its **limits**.
Save a few hundred a month and help Yusuf grow the garage.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a plan, like packing for a long journey.
S3.quote: I'd want to be able to tell my daughter to follow the path she wants, not the one we can afford, so I'd start now.
fieldNote: Esther becomes **methodical**: certificate, daily AI use, savings.
She wants her daughter's choices not tied to the family's money.
Her steady temperament makes five years feel workable.

steps.text: Take a supply-chain management certificate at night
Use AI at work every day to learn where it fails
Save three hundred a month for two months of cover
Start a children's education fund for Zara and Idris

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good length of time, so let's not panic. At work I'd say to keep learning. In the community I'd say teach children good habits and a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I feel hopeful but careful. By 2036 I'd be fifty-three, the mortgage nearly paid, and my children grown. I'd be doing a different version of this work, probably something with people at the centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and pay off debt faster. I'd study part-time for a qualification in supply chain or business, and I'd put money into a small family investment. I'd also keep an eye on how fast firms like mine change before I move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite calm. A decade is long enough for steady people like me to adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what do you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to have a skill that people will pay for and the discipline to keep learning. Work gives dignity, and I'd want that for my children. Hands, hearts and heads together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want younger people to be able to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The worry I carry is the near years, when money's tight. If we get through those, the ten-year plan is fine.

I'd say children should learn good habits and a trade.
think: I feel hopeful but careful; by 2036 the mortgage is nearly paid and the **kids** are grown.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It leaves no time to build a cushion, and my husband's income isn't steady enough to carry us. What would help is early notice from the owners, paid retraining, and apprenticeships so people can learn real skills while they earn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say steady people carry worry quietly. I follow the rules, I work hard, and I save when I can, and it still wouldn't take much to unsettle us.

headlineQuote: I follow the rules, I work hard, and I save when I can, and it still wouldn't take much to unsettle us.
portrait: Esther Rahman, 43, is a senior **buyer** of homeware for a wholesaler, with a garage-owner husband, two kids and a mortgage.
She's traditional, faith-minded and **steady**: she uses AI now and then and adopts tools once they're proven.
Her wage is the reliable one, with under a month saved, so even a quiet world leaves her uneasy.
She expects the thinking part of her job to go in the fast cases and prepares with **training** and savings.
She trusts family, community and honest work, and blames neither firms nor government alone.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because there's no time to build a cushion and Yusuf's income is uneven.
whatWouldHelp: Early **notice** from owners, paid retraining and apprenticeships where people earn while they learn.
